name: Changunarayan
tagline: The valley's oldest temple on a quiet ridge above Bhaktapur
meta_description: Changunarayan travel guide: Nepal's oldest dated inscription (464 CE), Vishnu temple, village museums, fees, how to reach from Bhaktapur and Kathmandu.
summary: Changunarayan is a Vishnu temple and Newar village on a 1,541 m ridge 6 km north of Bhaktapur, and one of the seven Kathmandu Valley UNESCO monument zones. It holds Nepal's oldest dated stone inscription (464 CE). Allow two to three hours, or walk down to Bhaktapur afterwards in about two hours.
intro: Most visitors reach Changunarayan almost by accident, tacked onto a Bhaktapur day or the end of a Nagarkot hike, and most leave wishing they had given it longer. The temple sits at the top of a single cobbled lane on Dolagiri hill, with forest behind it and the whole eastern half of the Kathmandu Valley below. There is no traffic in the lane and no tour-bus car park at the top. What you get instead is the oldest continuously worshipped temple site in the valley, a courtyard of fifth- to seventh-century sculpture, and a working village of brick houses around it.

The written history here is unusually precise. A stone pillar in the courtyard carries an inscription of the Licchavi king Manadeva dated 464 CE, the earliest dated record yet found in Nepal. The two-storey pagoda you see today was rebuilt in 1702 after a fire, and its roof struts carry carved multi-armed deities that reward a slow walk around all four sides. The 25 April 2015 earthquake cracked walls across the complex; restoration has since put the main shrine and most of the rest houses back into use.

We usually pair Changunarayan with Bhaktapur, 6 km and about 25 minutes away by road, or bring guests down here on foot from Nagarkot along the ridge through Telkot. Mornings are best: the light falls on the west face of the temple, priests are busy with the first puja, and the lane is still quiet. October to February brings the clearest air and views north to the Himalaya on good days. In the monsoon, June to September, the temple stays open but the trails turn to mud and the hills vanish into cloud.

highlights.title: The Manadeva pillar of 464 CE
highlights.text: Beside the west door of the main temple stands a stone pillar carrying a Sanskrit inscription of King Manadeva dated 464 CE. It records how he talked his widowed mother out of following her husband onto the funeral pyre, then rode out on campaign. It is the oldest dated inscription found in Nepal.

highlights.title: Licchavi sculpture in the courtyard
highlights.text: Scattered around the courtyard are stone reliefs carved between the fifth and seventh centuries: Vishnu as Vikranta striding across the three worlds, a many-headed Vishwarupa, and Narasimha tearing apart the demon Hiranyakashipu. Few places in South Asia let you stand this close to sculpture of this age without glass or barriers.

highlights.title: Garuda kneeling before Vishnu
highlights.text: A stone Garuda, Vishnu's bird mount, kneels on a low pedestal facing the west door with his hands folded in salutation. Pilgrims touch his base before going in. The figure is among the oldest in the complex and gives the courtyard its axis, so start your circuit here.

highlights.title: Carved roof struts on four sides
highlights.text: Each roof strut of the 1702 pagoda carries a painted wooden deity, many with ten or more arms, and the four doors are framed in gilded copper. Walk the full circuit clockwise and look up: the north and east sides are less photographed but just as finely worked.

highlights.title: A village lane of museums and tea shops
highlights.text: The 300 m lane up from the bus stop is lined with Newar brick houses, thangka and woodcarving shops, and two small museums: the family-run Changu Museum and the Living Traditions Museum, which reopened after earthquake repairs. Tea, momo and buffalo curd are sold from ground-floor kitchens along the way.

highlights.title: Ridge walks to Bhaktapur and Nagarkot
highlights.text: Changunarayan sits on two of the valley's best short walks. Downhill to Bhaktapur takes about two hours through terraced rice and mustard fields. Uphill along the ridge via Telkot reaches Nagarkot in four to five hours, and many of our guests do that route in reverse, ending with lunch here.

how_to_reach.text: Changunarayan is ≈ 22 km from Thamel, 1–1.5 h by car via Bhaktapur depending on Kathmandu traffic. From Bhaktapur it is ≈ 6 km and 20–30 minutes up a winding paved road. Local buses run from Bhaktapur's Kamal Binayak stop roughly every 30 minutes for about NPR 40. Cars park at the bottom of the village lane; the last 300 m is a gentle walk.

Two trails reach the temple. From Bhaktapur, walk north across the Manohara river and climb through fields for ≈ 6 km, about 2 hours uphill or 1.5 hours down. From Nagarkot, the ridge route via Telkot is ≈ 12 km and 4–5 hours, mostly downhill, on dirt road and forest path.

The nearest airport is Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu, about 18 km west. From the terminal, a private car takes 45 minutes to an hour via the Bhaktapur road, so Changunarayan works well as a first-afternoon outing for guests landing before noon.

where_to_stay: Most travellers visit Changunarayan as a half-day trip and sleep elsewhere. Bhaktapur, 25 minutes below, has small guesthouses inside the old town, which keeps the evening atmosphere close at hand. For mountain views, we base guests at Nagarkot, 45 minutes up the ridge road, and send them down to Changunarayan on foot the next morning. Kathmandu hotels in Thamel or Lazimpat put you 1–1.5 hours away by car. The village itself has a handful of family homestays and simple guesthouses along the temple lane, suitable for a quiet night with home-cooked Newar food; we arrange these on request rather than as a standard stop.
tips: Arrive before 9 am to see the morning puja and to photograph the west face of the temple in soft light.
Carry small notes: the entry ticket, museum fees and village tea shops all prefer cash in Nepali rupees.
Leather belts and shoes should be removed before stepping onto the temple plinth, and photography inside the sanctum is not allowed.
If you plan to walk down to Bhaktapur, keep your Bhaktapur heritage ticket money ready, since the trail enters the fee zone at the north edge of town.
Ekadashi days, especially Haribodhini Ekadashi in October or November, bring crowds of Vishnu devotees, so plan for a busier courtyard on those dates.

experiences.title: Changunarayan temple and 464 CE inscription
experiences.price_hint: Included in our Bhaktapur day tours
experiences.summary: A guided circuit of the Changunarayan courtyard, reading the Licchavi sculpture and the Manadeva pillar of 464 CE with a guide who knows the stories behind each relief. We time it for the morning puja, when the temple is busiest with local worshippers.
body: We start at the stone Garuda on the west side, the line every pilgrim follows, and then cross to the inscription pillar beside the main door. Your guide reads out the substance of the Sanskrit text: King Manadeva's father has died, his mother Rajyavati resolves to join him on the pyre, and the young king persuades her to live before setting out on campaigns east and west. Dated 464 CE, it is the earliest firm date in Nepali history, and it pins this hilltop as a royal shrine at least sixteen centuries ago.

From the pillar, we work clockwise around the pagoda. The reliefs in the courtyard corners are the reason art historians come: Vishnu Vikranta, his leg raised mid-stride across heaven, earth and the underworld; the ten-headed Vishwarupa, layered with smaller figures; and a Narasimha with the demon king across his knees. Several are carved from single slabs and date from the fifth to the seventh century. Your guide also points out the gilded door frames, the roof struts of 1702 and the smaller shrines to Chinnamasta and Krishna.

Hindu visitors can enter the sanctum doorway for darshan of Vishnu; the inner image is not photographed, and the priests ask for silence during aarti. Non-Hindus are welcome in the courtyard and on the plinth. Entry is NPR 400 for foreign visitors and NPR 300 for SAARC nationals, including Indians, as we last confirmed; check current status before you travel. The full circuit takes 90 minutes at a relaxed pace, longer if you want to sketch or photograph the sculpture in detail.

faqs.a: Non-Hindus can enter the courtyard, walk the plinth and photograph the exterior and sculpture freely. Only Hindu devotees step to the sanctum doorway for darshan, and no one photographs the inner image. In practice this restriction costs visitors very little, because the inscription, the reliefs and the carved struts are all outside the shrine itself.

faqs.q: What does the Changunarayan inscription say?
faqs.a: It is a royal record by King Manadeva, dated 464 CE, written in Sanskrit verse. It tells how his widowed mother, Queen Rajyavati, wished to follow her husband in death, how Manadeva persuaded her to live, and how he then led military campaigns to the east and west. It is the oldest dated inscription so far found in Nepal.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Changunarayan?
faqs.a: Allow 1.5 to 2 hours for the temple courtyard with a guide, plus 30 to 60 minutes for the village lane and a museum. If you add the walk down to Bhaktapur, budget a half day in total. Photographers who want both morning and late-afternoon light sometimes stay overnight in a village homestay.

experiences.title: Changu village lane and museum walk
experiences.best_time: Late morning, any month except heavy-rain days
experiences.summary: A slow walk up the brick lane that leads to the temple, with stops at the family-run Changu Museum, the Living Traditions Museum and the workshops of local woodcarvers and thangka painters. It shows the everyday village that has looked after this shrine for generations.
body: The lane from the bus stop to the temple gate is only about 300 m long, but it is the best place in the valley to see a Newar hill village that still runs on its own rhythm. Ground floors open onto the street as shops and kitchens; upper floors keep their carved wooden windows. You will pass rest houses, small Ganesh shrines and a stone water spout where women still wash vegetables in the morning. Several houses were rebuilt after 2015 with traditional brick and timber, and your guide can point out the old and new work side by side.

Halfway up, the Changu Museum is a family collection in an old house: coins, household tools, farm implements, weapons, ritual objects and kitchen vessels, many explained by members of the family who assembled it. Near the temple, the Living Traditions Museum shows everyday and ceremonial objects from communities across Nepal, from the Terai to the high mountains, in a restored rest house. Both are small, which is part of their appeal; give each 20 to 40 minutes.

We finish with tea or a plate of buffalo curd and beaten rice at one of the kitchens near the temple, and a look into a woodcarving or thangka workshop if the artists are working. Museum fees have been around NPR 200 to 300 per person, payable in cash; check current status before you travel. Opening hours are roughly 9 am to 5 pm, and the museums sometimes close on public holidays, so we confirm on the day.

faqs.q: Is the Changu Museum worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you enjoy small, personal collections. The Changu Museum is a family-run house of old coins, tools, ritual objects and household items, often explained by the family themselves. It takes 20 to 40 minutes and gives context to the village you have just walked through. Visitors expecting a large, formal museum should adjust their expectations.

faqs.q: Is the Living Traditions Museum at Changunarayan open?
faqs.a: It reopened after long earthquake repairs and was operating at our last check, displaying everyday and ceremonial objects from communities across Nepal. Hours and closures change, particularly on public holidays, so we confirm on the morning of your visit. Check current status before you travel if the museum is your main reason for coming.

faqs.q: Can I eat lunch in Changunarayan village?
faqs.a: Yes. Small family kitchens along the temple lane serve dal bhat, momo, chow mein, tea and the local buffalo curd with beaten rice. Expect simple food and prices of roughly NPR 300 to 700 per person. There is no hotel restaurant in the village, so for a longer sit-down lunch we usually eat in Bhaktapur afterwards.

experiences.title: Walk from Changunarayan down to Bhaktapur
experiences.price_hint: ≈ ₹2,500 per person with guide and car pick-up
experiences.summary: An easy 6 km walk from the temple ridge down through terraced fields, across the Manohara river and into the north side of Bhaktapur. It drops about 200 m to the river before a short climb into town, suits most fitness levels and turns a drive-in visit into a proper half-day outing.
body: We leave from the temple's south gate and drop down stone steps through the village, past the last houses and onto a path between terraces. In October and November the rice is gold and being harvested; from December to February the fields switch to mustard and wheat, and the views north stay clear longer into the day. The path is a mix of stone steps, farm track and short paved stretches, with no hard climbs on the way down.

After about 45 minutes the trail reaches the Manohara river, crossed on a road bridge, and then rises gently through brick kilns and small farms toward Bhaktapur. The total distance is about 6 km and the walk takes 1.5 to 2 hours with photo stops; the height drop from Changunarayan at 1,541 m to the river is roughly 200 m, then a short climb into Bhaktapur at about 1,400 m. Sturdy shoes are enough; trekking poles help on the steps if your knees complain.

You enter Bhaktapur on its northern edge and walk on to Taumadhi or Durbar Square, where foreign visitors pay the Bhaktapur heritage fee of about NPR 1,800 and SAARC nationals about NPR 500; check current status before you travel. Our driver meets you in Bhaktapur, so there is no need to return uphill. In the monsoon, from June to September, the field paths turn slippery and leeches appear, and we usually suggest driving instead.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Changunarayan to Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: It is about 6 km and takes 1.5 to 2 hours downhill with photo stops, or 2 to 2.5 hours in the uphill direction. The route crosses fields and the Manohara river on mostly easy paths and farm tracks. Our driver collects you in Bhaktapur so you do not need to walk back.

faqs.q: Can children and seniors do the Changunarayan to Bhaktapur walk?
faqs.a: Most children over about six and active seniors manage it comfortably, because the route is largely downhill and has no exposed sections. The stone steps below the village are the steepest part. Our guides walk at your pace, and the car can meet you at the river road if anyone wants to stop halfway.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to walk from Changunarayan to Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: The path is not technically difficult, but several farm tracks branch off and there are no signposts, so first-time visitors often lose time. A guide also explains the villages and fields along the way and arranges the pick-up in Bhaktapur. Independent walkers should download an offline map before starting.

Changunarayan is famous as the oldest temple site in the Kathmandu Valley and one of its seven UNESCO monument zones. Its courtyard holds Nepal's oldest dated inscription, King Manadeva's pillar of 464 CE, along with Licchavi stone sculpture from the fifth to seventh centuries. The present two-storey Vishnu pagoda was rebuilt in 1702 and is known for its carved roof struts.

faqs.q: What is the Changunarayan entry fee for Indians?
faqs.a: Indian visitors pay the SAARC rate, which was NPR 300 per person at our last check, while other foreign visitors pay NPR 400. That is about ₹190 at the fixed rate of 1.6 NPR to the rupee. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel and carry cash in Nepali rupees.

faqs.q: How far is Changunarayan from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Changunarayan is about 22 km east of central Kathmandu, which takes 1 to 1.5 hours by car depending on traffic through the city and Bhaktapur. From Tribhuvan Airport it is closer, about 45 minutes to an hour. Most visitors combine it with Bhaktapur, just 6 km below the temple ridge.

faqs.q: Can I visit Changunarayan and Bhaktapur in one day?
faqs.a: Yes, and we recommend it. Start at Changunarayan in the morning, spend about two hours at the temple and village, then drive 25 minutes or walk two hours down to Bhaktapur for lunch and the afternoon in the squares. Back in Kathmandu by evening, the whole day runs about eight to nine hours.

faqs.q: Was Changunarayan damaged in the 2015 earthquake?
faqs.a: Yes. The earthquake of 25 April 2015 cracked walls, toppled rest houses and damaged the museums around the courtyard. The main pagoda stayed standing, and restoration since then has returned the shrine and most of the surrounding buildings to use. Some smaller structures were still being repaired at our last visit, but the site is fully open to visitors.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Changunarayan?
faqs.a: The temple is open daily from early morning until around dusk, roughly 6 am to 6 pm, with the ticket booth staffed through the day. Morning, before 9 am, is the best time to see puja and avoid groups. Hours can change for festivals and special rituals, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Changunarayan included in the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO site?
faqs.a: Yes. Changu Narayan is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1979, together with the Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, Swayambhunath, Boudhanath and Pashupatinath. It is the only zone set in a village rather than in a city or large shrine complex.

faqs.q: Is the Nagarkot to Changunarayan hike difficult?
faqs.a: No, it is an easy to moderate walk of about 12 km and four to five hours, mainly downhill from Nagarkot at about 2,175 m to Changunarayan at 1,541 m. The route follows the ridge via Telkot on dirt roads and forest paths. It suits anyone used to walking a few hours; we send a guide and arrange the car at the end.

faqs.q: What should I wear to Changunarayan temple?
faqs.a: Wear clothing that covers shoulders and knees, as at any active Hindu temple, and shoes you can slip off easily, since you remove them before stepping onto the temple plinth. Leather belts and bags are best left in the car. In winter mornings, from December to February, a warm layer helps, as the ridge sits around 5 to 8 °C at dawn.
